extracted.intended_audience: grant program designers, panel chairs, funders, and researchers studying peer review and grant deliberation
extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative guidance on how grant-review panels in the humanities and social sciences actually evaluate proposals, including both explicit criteria and tacit judgments observed in deliberations. Useful for designing rubrics, training reviewers, and structuring panel procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proposal break new ground intellectually?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary consensus criterion; panels look for intellectual novelty as a core measure of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the question matter to the field or beyond?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses the topical importance and potential impact of the proposed research on the discipline and broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods / clarity of approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research design coherent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates methodological appropriateness and whether the proposal clearly explains how it will pursue its questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the applicant pull this off?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges likelihood of successful completion given time, resources, and applicant capabilities; often informed by 'promise' judgments about the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and social significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work speak to broader concerns?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses relevance beyond narrow disciplinary contribution—cultural resonance, social relevance, or public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived passion, dedication, commitment in the proposal voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tacit, affective judgment about the applicant's engagement and seriousness; panels frequently infer commitment from tone, narrative, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance / aesthetic appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic presentation or elegance of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists sometimes favor proposals that are written or framed with stylistic polish or conceptual elegance; aesthetic preferences can influence decisions beyond technical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the applicant seem to 'own' the question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges whether the project feels genuinely rooted in the applicant's intellectual trajectory or voice; authenticity can increase perceived credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived future potential of the applicant as a scholar (separable from the proposal itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists assess applicant trajectory, potential for future contributions, and whether funding would help an emerging scholar develop a career; this can outweigh or color proposal-specific judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic, institutional, demographic balance across awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels often take portfolio-level diversity into account when allocating awards, including representation by region, institution type, career stage, or demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic balance in the awarded portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders and panels may aim for a balanced portfolio across topics, approaches, and applicants; decisions can reflect program-level strategy rather than only per-proposal merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying field-appropriate evaluation standards; judging proposals within their field's standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists emphasize evaluating work according to disciplinary epistemologies and norms rather than applying a single cross-disciplinary standard; this is both a tacit criterion and a procedural norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizes interpretive, social-constructionist framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists with this style value interpretive richness, context-sensitive analysis, and theoretical framing that foregrounds social constructions; appropriate for qualitative and interpretive projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: Values broad synthesis, integration across domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists favor proposals that synthesize disparate literatures or bridge domains; they prize scope and integrative ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivist epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: Values methodological rigor, hypothesis testing, replicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists prioritizing this style look for clear methods, empirical testability, and reproducibility; they reward formal rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: Values practical applicability and policy relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists with a utilitarian orientation emphasize practical outcomes, usefulness, and potential policy or societal applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The in-field panelist's view weighs heavily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural norm where domain experts influence or anchor deliberations; chairs and panels often rely on specialized members for substantive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking turns and avoiding dominance in discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms intended to ensure equitable participation and prevent any single member from unduly controlling decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting that multiple approaches can be excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels often permit different epistemological or methodological standards to coexist; fair evaluation recognizes diverse valid approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic horse-trading
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal reciprocal support ('I'll support yours if you support mine') within informal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge existence of bargaining and trade-offs in allocation decisions; panels may use informal deals to achieve portfolio goals while staying within ethical/procedural bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attack absent applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm to keep deliberations focused on proposals and professional judgments rather than personal criticisms of applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow discipline-specific epistemological norms in rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubrics should make space for discipline-specific epistemological norms rather than applying a single universal standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: include fields or guidance that let reviewers evaluate according to the field-appropriate criteria (e.g., interpretive depth for humanities, reproducibility for positivist work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'promise' / aesthetic / character judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that 'promise', aesthetic appeal, and character-like judgments happen and should be accommodated in rubric design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: rubrics can include explicit items or narrative fields for reviewer impressions of applicant potential, engagement, and presentation quality to surface tacit judgments transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include procedural norms of deliberation in review systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubrics and panel procedures should account for norms (deference, turn-taking, pluralism, limits on bargaining) that structure deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: train chairs/reviewers on deliberation norms, create mechanisms to manage expertise deference and portfolio-level balancing, and document acceptable trade-offs.
